title: SQLite for Crawl Pipelines: Idempotency, WAL, and Bounded Concurrency
seoTitle: SQLite Crawl Pipelines: Idempotent Writes and WAL
subtitle: Serialize writes without losing attempts, evidence, or recovery paths.
seoDescription: Design SQLite crawl storage around one writer, stable keys and append-only attempts. Bound transactions, manage WAL checkpoints and test backup restoration.

artwork.alt: Parallel monochrome data streams converge through a single writer into concentric WAL-like records.
artwork.label: Data systems / single-writer study
artwork.caption: Bounded workers converge on one durable writer while layered records preserve recovery and replay.

author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: SQLite suits bounded crawls when writes are idempotent, attempts remain immutable, and current-state projections cannot move backwards. Accept one-writer semantics and operate WAL, checkpoints, and recovery deliberately.

conclusion.title: Prove the database can be restored
conclusion.content: Idempotent writes and ordered projections protect collection; short transactions and deliberate checkpoints protect operation. Complete the storage contract with integrity checks, stable exports, and a restoration that reproduces run counts and report results.

evidenceBoundary: SQLite behavior depends on the linked library version, VFS, filesystem, durability settings, connection pattern, and workload. Official documentation should be rechecked before deployment; WAL is not a shared-database design for independent hosts or a substitute for backups.
content: Crawler workers finish out of order. Retries redeliver results, browser artifacts arrive after source captures, and reports read while collection continues. Shared connections, per-row commits, replacement writes, and overwritten status tables can turn that concurrency into duplicate work or lost history.

Narrow the write boundary instead. Workers emit immutable result messages; a single writer or serialized writer service validates and commits bounded batches before acknowledging them. Stable keys make redelivery safe, append-only attempts keep history, and rebuildable projections serve reporting.

sections.title: Define what each row represents
paragraphs: Give every table one grain: crawl_run is a bounded execution; url_identity a comparison key under a normalizer version; discovery_edge an observed source relation; fetch_attempt a request attempt; response_artifact a saved payload; rule_evaluation a rule version on an input set. Mixed grains make retries and uniqueness ambiguous.

Use local surrogate IDs where helpful, but constrain domain identity explicitly. Attempts can be unique by run, URL, and sequence, or by a scheduler-generated idempotent attempt ID. Artifacts need hash plus storage namespace; link edges need source artifact and node identity to retain repeated-template context.

Keep normalized query fields alongside immutable evidence. A normalized canonical groups pages while the observed href explains it; integer statuses support queries while raw headers remain hashed artifacts. Model core relations explicitly without discarding JSON when it faithfully captures the source.

table.caption: Recommended crawl-storage grains
rows: One comparison key under one normalizer
run + source artifact + node + observed ref
One rule version on one input set
run + URL + rule + version + input hash

sections.title: Commit the durable result as one unit
paragraphs: A completed fetch can produce attempt state, response metadata, artifact references, observations, edges, and frontier transitions. Explicitly commit the records forming one durable result together, or define a resumable sequence with valid intermediate states.

Per-row transactions amplify synchronization overhead; whole-crawl transactions hold the writer, defer visibility, enlarge recovery, and make failure costly. Bound batches by messages, bytes, or time and checkpoint which messages committed.

Avoid network and filesystem waits inside transactions. Persist the artifact first, then commit its immutable reference briefly. Storage failure leaves the result retryable; commit failure permits redelivery because uniqueness prevents duplicate logical records.
bullets: Begin and end transactions in the writer, not inside unrelated helper functions.
Keep every transaction bounded by records, bytes, and wall time.
Do not wait on HTTP, browser, or remote object storage while holding the writer.
Acknowledge a worker result only after the durable transaction commits.
Record the result-message ID used for deduplication.
Retry SQLITE_BUSY with a bounded policy rather than an infinite loop.

sections.title: Advance projections without replacing evidence
paragraphs: Redelivering a logical result should converge on the same durable state. Use a unique message or domain key with INSERT and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for immutable first commits. Reserve DO UPDATE for projections with explicit update policies.

INSERT OR REPLACE can delete and recreate rows, affect foreign keys, change identity, and erase first observations. Named conflict targets and selected update columns state which collision is expected and which values may change.

Late messages must not overwrite newer terminal attempts. Guard updates with sequence, event time under a documented clock policy, or state version in the WHERE clause. Retain each attempt even when it cannot advance the projection.

codeExamples.title: Append and project
codeExamples.description: Duplicate result delivery becomes a no-op, and late attempts cannot move current state backward.

sections.title: Control the writer and long-lived readers
paragraphs: WAL lets readers continue while a writer appends commits, but still permits one writer at a time. Serialize worker results, keep transactions short, bound busy waits or retries, and expose queue age to apply backpressure rather than adding competing writers.

Readers retain transaction snapshots. Long reports can prevent checkpoint progress and grow WAL. Close reads promptly, paginate exports against deliberate snapshots, and monitor WAL pages and checkpoint results. SQLite’s documentation explains automatic checkpoints and the write-latency, read-performance, and durability tradeoffs.

WAL’s shared-memory design requires participating processes on the same host; its documentation warns against network filesystems. For independent machines, put write authority behind a service or use a server database. Copying the main file alone during live WAL can omit committed data: backup and archive procedures must respect journal mode.

table.caption: SQLite crawl concurrency responsibilities
rows: Retry delivery, not direct database mutation
Cancel or move long export to snapshot copy
Investigate long readers and write bursts

sections.title: Test interruption, export, and restoration
paragraphs: Interrupt before artifact storage, between storage and commit, during a batch, between commit and acknowledgment, and during reporting. Expect either no committed logical change or one complete idempotent result. Normal runs cannot demonstrate those recovery boundaries.

Schedule quick or full integrity checks for the workload and important archives; check foreign keys separately where used. Back up with a supported SQLite mechanism or controlled closed/checkpointed state, not an informal copy of changing files.

Order exports explicitly and include schema version, run manifest, counts, hashes, and gaps. SQL dumps preserve relations; CSV and JSON support review. Restore the archive and compare run counts and key report queries before declaring it complete.
bullets: Pin or inventory the actual SQLite library version used in production.
Review current official advisories before relying on WAL behavior.
Exercise crash and duplicate-delivery tests against the writer.
Monitor queue age, commit latency, WAL size, and checkpoint progress.
Run integrity and foreign-key checks before durable archive.
Restore a backup and compare deterministic report hashes.
